questions.q: Per this lesson, why does treating every board question as a personal attack make a presenter's defense weaker, not stronger?
options: Boards automatically fail anyone who seems nervous
Reviewers can feel the difference between someone explaining their reasoning and someone protecting their pride, and defending yourself instead of the design's logic reads as weaker
It is against the rules to respond defensively in any review board
There is no actual difference in how either approach is received
questions.explain: A question about a design is a request for the reasoning behind it, not a verdict on the presenter -- answering the reasoning reads as stronger than defending one's own competence or pride.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say tying every decision to a stated requirement in advance is the single most effective defense?
options: Because most challenging questions are really asking 'why this and not the alternative' or 'what requirement demanded this,' and a decision already connected to a requirement just needs restating, not a new argument built live
Because requirements documents are the only thing a board is allowed to ask about
Because decisions based on general best practice are always the easiest to defend
Because tying decisions to requirements removes the need to ever answer a follow-up question
questions.explain: If a decision is already connected to a specific requirement from the presentation, defending it under questioning just restates a connection the board already heard -- decisions justified only by abstract 'best practice' are the hardest to defend because there's nothing concrete to point back to.

questions.q: What makes an answer about 'the road not taken' land as architectural judgment rather than a strawman, per this lesson?
options: Dismissing the alternative outright as simply worse, with no further explanation
Refusing to discuss any alternative that wasn't chosen
Naming the alternative accurately, stating the specific reason it didn't fit this scenario's constraints, without implying it was a bad idea in general
Claiming the alternative was never considered at all
questions.explain: Accurately naming the alternative and explaining why this specific scenario's constraints made it the wrong fit -- without implying it's generally a bad idea -- shows real evaluation of tradeoffs, while dismissing it outright reads as not having seriously considered it.

questions.q: Which trait does this lesson identify as separating a defense that holds up under scrutiny from a rehearsed-sounding one?
options: A rehearsed defense always covers follow-up questions better because it was prepared in advance
A defense built from underlying reasoning adapts to a rephrased question; one built from memorized phrasing unravels when the question is asked differently
There is no meaningful difference between the two under real questioning
A good defense should recite the identical phrase regardless of how a question is worded
questions.explain: A rehearsed-sounding defense tends to break down the moment a reviewer rephrases the question or asks a follow-up the memorized answer doesn't cover, because it was never built from the actual reasoning -- only the words.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe conceding a genuine gap well as a defensive skill rather than a failure?
options: Because a candidate who honestly names a gap and sketches how they'd address it demonstrates exactly the judgment a board is evaluating, often worth more than a design with no gaps at all
Because conceding a point always counts as an automatic failure on a review board
Because boards never ask questions that expose a genuine design gap
Because manufacturing a justification on the spot is always preferable to admitting a limitation
questions.explain: Treating every challenge as something to win is itself a mistake a sharp board notices. Honestly naming a real gap and how you'd close it demonstrates the architectural judgment boards are actually trying to evaluate.
